sysd-blocks-129.title: Proxy server: the intermediary in the middle
sysd-blocks-129.text:
Sometimes the best way to reach a server is not to talk to it directly. A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it. The client directs the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions. That indirection controls complexity or adds benefits such as load balancing, privacy or security. A proxy may sit on the user's own computer or at any point between the user's computer and the destination servers.

Proxies typically filter requests, log them, or transform them by adding or removing headers, encrypting or decrypting, or compressing. Proxies may add headers such as X-Forwarded-For, or the standardised Forwarded field, to pass on client information. These should not be trusted blindly, because they may be absent, modified or added by several proxies. A proxy works at layer 7 of the OSI model. Network address translation is similar but works at layer 3, so it is less resource-intensive and less flexible.

sysd-blocks-130.title: Forward proxy: a middleman for clients
sysd-blocks-130.text:
A forward proxy is a middleman for clients: no origin server ever communicates directly with them. It is a server that sits in front of a group of client machines and communicates with Internet servers on their behalf. When the clients request sites and services on the Internet, the proxy intercepts the requests and talks to the web servers for them. It can regulate traffic by preset policies, convert and mask client IP addresses, enforce security protocols and block unknown traffic, which strengthens policy enforcement inside an internal network.

Common uses are blocking access to certain content, reaching geo-restricted content, providing anonymity and avoiding other browsing restrictions. An anonymous proxy reveals that it is a proxy but does not disclose the client's originating IP address. Web filtering proxies cannot see inside HTTPS unless managed clients are configured to trust a root certificate whose private key the proxy knows. Proxies bring anonymity but can still track personal information, and setting one up and maintaining it can be costly.

sysd-blocks-137.title: Reverse proxy: a front door for servers
sysd-blocks-137.text:
A reverse proxy, also called a surrogate server, appears to clients to be an ordinary web server. It merely forwards their requests to one or more ordinary web servers. It returns the original server's response as if it came from the proxy itself, so the client never learns of the original server. The web servers can be hidden behind a firewall on the internal network, with only the reverse proxy exposed to the Internet. A forward proxy serves clients; a reverse proxy protects the servers.

By inspecting HTTP headers it can present a single IP address to the Internet while relaying requests to different internal servers by URL. It can balance load and often terminates TLS connections from clients, which centralizes certificate management, access control, logging and routing and reduces TLS work on backend servers. It can also cache static and dynamic content, greatly reducing the load on origin servers. Application firewall features can protect against denial-of-service attacks, but the proxy gives no protection against attacks on the web application itself.

sysd-blocks-191.title: HAProxy: an open source balancer and proxy
sysd-blocks-191.text: On 64-core ARM servers, HAProxy has reached 2 million requests per second and 100 Gbit/s. It is free, open source software that provides a high-availability load balancer and proxy for TCP and HTTP-based applications, spreading requests across multiple servers. It balances at layer 4 (TCP) and layer 7 (HTTP). It also offers SSL/TLS termination, URL rewriting, simplified circuit breaking, HTTP/2 on both sides and hitless reloads. Written in C with an event-driven multithreaded architecture, it has a reputation for speed and efficiency. Servers with 6 to 8 cores generally reach 200,000 to 500,000 requests per second.

sysd-blocks-133.title: API gateway: one entry point to many services
sysd-blocks-133.text:
Backend services built as small units typically expose fine-grained APIs, nothing like what a client needs, so clients would have to talk to several of them. An API gateway removes that burden. It is a tool for managing APIs. It sits between clients and a set of backend services as their single entry point, enforcing security and throttling policies before passing requests on.

Its core functions are routing requests to the appropriate backend service, load balancing, and API composition, which combines several backend API requests into one frontend request. It also handles security and traffic control: identity checks, data encryption, request-rate limits and throttling, and IP whitelisting or blacklisting. Resilience and visibility features include retries, circuit breaking, stored copies of frequent responses, logging, tracing and analytics. Its advantages are a hidden internal structure, a centralized view of the API and simpler client code. The disadvantages are one component whose failure could block all traffic, a possible performance impact, a bottleneck if not scaled properly, and challenging configuration.

sysd-blocks-132.title: Caching proxy: answering from saved copies
sysd-blocks-132.text: The caching proxy was the first kind of proxy server, and web proxies are commonly used to keep copies of web pages from a web server. A caching proxy speeds up requests by returning content saved from an earlier request by the same or another client. Keeping local copies of frequently requested resources lets large organizations significantly cut upstream bandwidth use and costs while significantly increasing performance. Poorly implemented ones can cause problems, such as an inability to identify users. A Performance Enhancing Proxy goes after link problems instead, for example improving TCP performance under high round-trip times or packet loss.

sysd-blocks-190.title: Nginx: a web server that also proxies and balances
sysd-blocks-190.text:
A single nginx server can hold more than 10,000 simultaneous connections, using about 2.5 MB per 10k inactive keep-alive connections. It does so by handling requests asynchronously, driven by events rather than threads, which gives predictable performance under high load. The nginx web server can also act as a reverse proxy, load balancer, mail proxy and HTTP cache. It can serve static content, act as a proxy server and serve dynamic content through FastCGI, SCGI, WSGI servers or Phusion Passenger. As a software load balancer, it offers in-band health checks.

It supports HTTP/2, including as an upstream protocol, and experimental HTTP/3. It was written to be faster than Apache, which has offered similar performance since version 2.4. Its speed came at the cost of flexibility, such as no per-file access overrides like Apache's .htaccess. It can upgrade its executable and configuration without losing client connections, and the paid NGINX Plus adds advanced load balancing.

sysd-blocks-131.title: Transparent proxy: a proxy clients do not choose
sysd-blocks-131.text: A transparent proxy is one the client never chose, and may never notice. Also called an intercepting proxy, it redirects or filters client traffic without being explicitly selected by the client. It is often deployed without browser or application proxy settings and commonly redirects outgoing TCP port 80 traffic. Businesses use intercepting proxies to enforce acceptable use policies without configuring client browsers. ISPs in some countries use them to save upstream bandwidth by keeping copies of content. Interception raises problems: the original destination IP and port must reach the proxy, HTTP logins such as NTLM break, and some responses become uncacheable by a shared cache.

sysd-blocks-138.title: Reverse proxy trade-offs: a single door is a single risk
sysd-blocks-138.text: A reverse proxy is a single door to the servers behind it, which makes it a risk as well as a shield. Misconfiguration, a denial-of-service attack or a software fault can make every frontend service unreachable, and adding spare proxies increases complexity further. To filter, cache or compress encrypted traffic, the proxy must decrypt and re-encrypt it. That needs the TLS certificate and private key, extends the number of systems with access to unencrypted data and makes the proxy a more valuable attack target. Giving a third party's reverse proxy access to private keys places confidentiality, integrity and availability in that party's hands.

sysd-blocks-134.title: API gateway request flow: stage by stage
sysd-blocks-134.text: A request to an API gateway has several hurdles to clear before any service sees it. The gateway parses and validates the request's attributes and runs allow-list and deny-list checks. It then consults an outside service that knows who the caller is, the idea behind {{ref:sysd-reliab-026}}. Next it applies rate-limit rules and rejects the request if it is over the limit. Once the basic checks pass, the gateway finds the relevant service by path matching, transforms the request into the appropriate protocol and sends it to the backend services. It can handle errors, and use circuit breaking for faults that take longer to recover.

sysd-blocks-136.title: Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer
sysd-blocks-136.text: Reverse proxies, API gateways and load balancers all sit in front of servers. Each suits a different job, and a system can use all three together. A reverse proxy keeps servers hidden from clients and shields sensitive websites from cyber-attacks. An API gateway delivers requests to the right services and suits busy applications with many intercommunicating services. A load balancer directs traffic evenly across servers to prevent bottlenecks, and it helps when several servers do the same job. A reverse proxy helps even with one server and can also balance load, but not the other way around.

sysd-blocks-135.title: Backend for frontend pattern: one backend per interface
sysd-blocks-135.text: Each frontend gets its own backend. The Backend For Frontend pattern creates a separate backend service for each specific frontend application or interface, which avoids customizing a single backend for multiple interfaces. Backend service output is often not in the exact format or filtering a front end needs. The pattern moves that reformatting logic from the frontend into an intermediate layer. Its primary function is to get the required data from the appropriate service, format it and send it to the frontend. Consider it when a shared general-purpose backend carries significant development overhead or should be optimized for one client.

sysd-blocks-189.title: API management: publishing, controlling and measuring an API
sysd-blocks-189.text: Publishing an API is only the start of running one. API management is the process of publishing APIs on the web, enforcing their usage policies, controlling access, supporting their users, and collecting and analyzing usage statistics and performance. Typical products combine a gateway, publishing tools, a developer portal or API store, reporting and analytics, and monetization. Publishing tools define, document, test and deploy APIs under access and usage policies. The developer portal gathers documentation, sample code, a sandbox and subscription-key management. Reporting analyzes usage and load, which helps optimize the API and set the service levels it promises.

openers.proxies-and-api-gateways: A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it. It can face two ways: a forward proxy sits in front of a group of client machines and speaks to the Internet for them, while a reverse proxy appears to clients to be an ordinary web server but merely forwards their requests on. Add a single entry point that enforces security and throttling policies before passing requests to backend services, and you have an API gateway. This chapter also meets caching and transparent proxies, the Backend For Frontend pattern, and two widely used tools, HAProxy and nginx.

reviews.proxies-and-api-gateways: This chapter is about things that stand between a client and a server. A forward proxy stands in for clients, a reverse proxy for servers, and a transparent proxy does it without the client choosing. A reverse proxy can balance load, terminate TLS and cache, and an API gateway adds identity checks, rate limits and routing to the right service. HAProxy and nginx are two real tools that do much of this, while the Backend For Frontend pattern gives each interface its own backend. The price of the single door is a single risk, so the choice among a reverse proxy, an API gateway and a load balancer depends on the job at hand.
